## Teaching philosophy

My teaching begins with a simple question: how can students see why a political question matters to them? Political science courses often ask students to engage unfamiliar theories, institutions, and cases. I design classes that first connect abstract political questions to problems students recognize in their own lives and the world around them, and then ask students to use theory and evidence to explain those problems.

I developed this approach while leading discussion sections for Introduction to Political Theory. Rather than asking students to react only to abstract concepts, I began with concrete political conflicts and contemporary cases. For example, when discussing Thomas Aquinas's account of just war, I asked students to consider how its principles might apply to the war in Ukraine. When discussing equality, I introduced a contemporary campus controversy in South Korea involving women's education and a proposed transition to coeducation. These cases gave students a clearer reason to participate and helped them connect foundational political ideas to real-world problems.

## Teaching methods and evidence

I use the same principle in methods teaching. In POLS-Y205 Political Analysis, I gave short “Evaluating Claims” lectures in which students used empirical evidence to assess claims they might encounter in media or everyday life. In one session, I began with a question about whether parents influence their children's political leanings and then used the study behind that question to show how a research design supports or limits a claim.

Elisabeth Brannon, the course instructor, described these sessions as “clear and thorough, as well as engaging,” adding that “Students visibly perked up during these sessions and were excited by the material he covered.” She also noted that I “patiently and clearly walked students through material that they struggled with” during lab exercises.  
*Elisabeth Brannon, POLS-Y205 Teaching Observation, 2026*

The official Y205 course evaluations asked students to evaluate the Associate Instructors collectively rather than individually. Selected comments on the instructional team included:

- “The AIs would evaluate claims with the class, which I enjoyed.”
- “The AIs were fair graders and kind, and their lectures were a good way to break up regular class instruction.”
- “The AIs for the course were very available and helpful.”

A second principle of my teaching is that students should be able to explain complex ideas in their own words. I use short handwritten reflections and oral explanations as low-stakes checks for comprehension. Familiarity with terminology is not the same as understanding; students should be able to explain what they know clearly and revise their explanations after discussion.

## Community-engaged learning

I also want students to apply political science to real policy problems outside the classroom. In a Public Policy or Urban Politics course, I would design a community engagement assignment in which students select a policy issue, review relevant research, and prepare questions before meeting with a local civic organization working on that issue. Afterward, students would write a report connecting what they learned from the organization to theories discussed in class and evaluating the issue using relevant evidence.

This approach builds on a housing politics course I took in the Geography department, where students investigated housing vulnerability and inequality in Indianapolis and engaged with local advocates, including the Indiana Women's Prison Alliance, around community-centered redevelopment and the future of the former Indiana Women's Prison site. That experience showed me how field-based work can make the institutional and distributional consequences of policy more concrete.
